text: Aferim, old man Velichkov! See, that’s how I like you. Why should we deceive the young generation? Let’s open our cards. Ideals! Nonsense! Our own personal earthly satisfaction—that is the ideal we should pursue. I’m glad that you have already arrived at this truth. And does this vile people deserve us to wear ourselves out for them! When we were younger, that was one thing; but now—we’ve become people over forty years old, we must think of ourselves. Enough of dry bread! Especially you, poor soul, you’ve really worn yourself out in those Istanbul alleys, in those Italian... wasn’t that a whole feat? When you saw that Stambolov had gone mad, you packed your bags and left Bulgaria, abandoned those slaves—let them spit in slavery. They’re used to it. You are not used to suffering, and like any gentleman you tried to make off. What didn’t your head suffer in that cursed Halki—and even for medicines, at times, you didn’t have enough money. Bobchev and Madzharov fell silent. Enough of feats already. And do you know what—just give up that cursed poetry of yours too. It’s all right, but only when the wind is blowing through your purse; and now, thank God, we’ve settled ourselves somewhat. They’ll start now, all sorts of brats, all sorts of little socialists, little idealists, to bark at you, but don’t let your eye even blink! Pretend not to hear, and look after your pleasure, and while you’re looking after your pleasure, smile at their brains. That’s how it is. Why would they bark at you? Surely for some betrayal of yours, for some fraud, out of disappointment? No! Out of envy? Of course! Without a doubt! Without a doubt, out of envy! And why? Simply because their bones were crushed, their throats were torn, while you (you’re a terrible devil, confound you!) just happened to drop in ready-made to the warmest place. Well, do you see now? Have you come around? Didn’t I tell you that in this world the best thing is to be warm and snug? All that social struggle, ideals, and I don’t know what nonsense—that’s all bosh! Just now, when you put your little bag down at the end of the month and they pour in a thousand and five hundred levs... A fine thing, by God! Hold on now! Once you’ve got the bone—hold it! Don’t you even think about whose skin those levs are being flayed from... Beat the flour sack, damn it! Beat it! It’s letting loose...

But you may be wondering why I am writing you this letter. I am writing it to praise you for your speech the other day in the National Assembly. Well done, Kocho! Honestly, I was moved to tears with joy. I almost came to you and kissed you in front of all the deputies. But then they would start stamping their feet at me, objecting... Do you remember which speech I mean? How could you not remember? The whole world is talking about it. But you are right, Kocho! So what if so many thousands of voters do not tear apart twenty gendarmes and fifty drunken thugs. Big deal! The gendarmes would have shot at most a hundred voters! Well, is that such a big deal? In all, only about two hundred houses would have been left in mourning. Let’s say that next Sunday the army comes and shoots, kills at most, at most three hundred people. How many orphaned houses would there be — five hundred houses! Hepidje maslahat!...

Well, those softies have started trying to pacify the crowd, so that not a hair should fall! How can one not be outraged?... Thanks to such weak-kneed softies, you waited a full eight years in Halki... To write them so many poems about the stars and about sighs, and for them to make you wait eight years. Eight years! A disgrace to the Bulgarian people. If only at least a hundred thousand voters from all over Bulgaria had gone under the bullets, you could have occupied your present warm place much earlier. But what a lousy people! Cowards! What the hell is this legality and freedom for, if at least a thousand voters are not exterminated?... Keep it up, dear Kocho, I like you that way. Give such speeches more often, so as to inspire greater confidence in the big bosses... and then mind your own pleasure! So what if the young generation is to be indignant, so what if the people are to be stirred up — don’t let your eye even blink! The people! The people are a herd; just swing the club at them... And after all, am I the one to teach you these things!...

I am most glad that it was you who hurried to deliver this speech; no one could get ahead of you. And now, if you have not inspired them with trust, where else could you!... All the rich men are praising you! Bravo, they say, Kocho has become one of us, at last he has come to his senses. So use your head now, hold on this time, and do not be afraid!... But still, mind you, Kocho, put some money aside, for one never knows — the world is a flower!

Kocho, when you read this letter, tear it up, so it doesn’t fall into the hands of that fellow who once described me traveling around Europe, because he’ll expose me somewhere again. I heard him the other day speaking to someone: “Well, what a pity, I really didn’t expect those words from our Velichkov”... and I listened to him and wondered at his mind. The wind blows him away... Kocho, why are you still publishing that cursed “Progress”? Give it up! Indeed, even its name is so childish; it no longer suits a solid man like you. And if you’re itching to write so much, then write, but it would be most fitting to call the newspaper “It’s Not the Time,” and then our partisans should be called “not-the-timeists.”
I brought a few bottles in my saddlebag. Can’t you whip up some little law so that public buildings can be sprinkled with rose oil?
